title: Untrusted Payload Conversion Bypassing Boundary or Domain Validation
pattern: Untrusted input becomes a domain object without enforcing required structural/format constraints, or deserialization directly constructs a domain representation while bypassing its business invariants and validated constructors.
why_bad: Malformed payloads or invalid business states reach code that assumes validity, spreading defensive validation and delaying errors beyond the input boundary.
detection: Subcase A: inspect derived/direct deserialization of core domain types, especially public mutable fields, for construction paths that skip invariant checks. Subcase B: trace field extraction from dynamic JSON/XML trees or DTO assembly and identify required fields, types, formats, or schema constraints that are not enforced before domain use. Implementing `Deserialize`, residing in a domain directory, or omitting an intermediate DTO alone does not prove a bypass.
counterexample:
Validated boundary representations followed by invariant-preserving domain construction are legitimate. Custom or validated deserialization that enforces the same checks can also safely construct domain values directly. Trusted internal persistence decoding (e.g. domain state round-tripped through a trusted database engine) is outside the untrusted-ingress case only when the relevant trust and invariant guarantees actually hold; schema validation alone does not prove all business invariants.
```rust
let schema: Schema = ...;
schema.validate(&dto)?;                 // structural/format checks at the boundary
let item = InventoryItem::new(dto)?;    // business invariants still enforced
```
source: *Domain Modeling made Functional* by Scott Wlaschin (Chapter 11, p. 245, "Deserialization Gates"); *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture* by Martin Fowler (p. 392).
